title: Roadmap 08: Spring Boot and FastAPI core
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: App startup and auto-configuration, dependency injection, REST routing and status codes, validation and DTOs, error handling, and filters, interceptors, AOP and middleware in Spring Boot and FastAPI.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

options.text: @Component, @EnableWebMvc, @Transactional and @Autowired together.
options.why: These are not the three that make up the annotation.

options.text: @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan.
options.why: Right: configuration class, auto-configuration and component scanning.

options.text: @RestController, @Service and @Repository, the stereotype annotations.
options.why: These are stereotypes found by component scanning.

options.text: @Bean, @Autowired and @Profile, which configure and wire beans.
options.why: These configure or wire beans, not the application class.

questions.explanation: Auto-configuration creates beans based on the classpath and your properties (starters bring the dependencies). Profiles select configuration such as application-dev.yml. FastAPI's counterpart is the app object plus APIRouter modules, with startup and shutdown work in a lifespan handler.

questions.prompt: Select all statements about dependency injection that are true.

options.text: Constructor injection allows final fields and lets a unit test build the class with plain mocks, without starting Spring.
options.why: Right: dependencies are explicit and required.

options.text: A Spring bean without an explicit @Scope is a singleton: one shared instance per application context.
options.why: Right: singleton is the default scope.

options.text: app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = fake_get_db replaces that dependency in FastAPI tests.
options.why: Right: the override is looked up by the original function.

options.text: A singleton Spring bean is one instance per JVM, even if several application contexts exist.
options.why: It is one instance per container, not per JVM.

options.text: FastAPI runs each Depends function once at startup and reuses the result for all requests.
options.why: Dependencies run per request; within one request the result is cached.

questions.explanation: IoC means the container creates and wires objects instead of your code calling new. Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies; use overrides and mocks to test in isolation.

options.text: 404, because no user with id abc exists.
options.why: The route matched; the 404 would need your own lookup code.

options.text: 400, because FastAPI maps every bad input to Bad Request.
options.why: FastAPI uses 422 for request validation errors.

options.text: 422, because abc is not a valid int path parameter.
options.why: Right: FastAPI returns a 422 body that names the failing field.

options.text: 500, because the int conversion raises an unhandled error.
options.why: Conversion errors are caught and reported as validation errors.

questions.explanation: Type hints drive parsing and validation: path parameters come from the URL, other simple parameters are query parameters (verbose here), and a Pydantic model is read from the body.

questions.prompt: A Spring @PostMapping endpoint creates a resource and should answer 201 Created with a Location header. Which return statement does that?

options.text: return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.OK).body(dto);
options.why: ok() produces 200 with no Location header.

options.text: return ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(dto);
options.why: Right: created(URI) sets 201 and the Location header.

options.text: return ResponseEntity.accepted().body(dto);
options.why: accepted() is 202, meaning work is queued, not created.

options.text: return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
options.why: noContent() is 204 and carries no body or Location.

questions.explanation: Build the URI from the new id, for example with ServletUriComponentsBuilder. FastAPI equivalents: status_code=201 on the decorator and a Response or header for Location.

questions.prompt: True or false: in a FastAPI request body model, raising ValueError inside a Pydantic field_validator makes FastAPI answer with a 422 response that names the failing field.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: Pydantic wraps the error and FastAPI turns it into a 422.

options.text: False
options.why: A validation failure does not become a 500 or a 400 by default.

questions.explanation: Pydantic v2 uses @field_validator (with @classmethod). In Spring the equivalent is Bean Validation: @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter plus constraints like @NotNull and @Size, which raise MethodArgumentNotValidException (400 by default).

questions.prompt: True or false: returning JPA entities directly from controllers is the recommended design, because DTOs only add mapping code.

options.text: True
options.why: Entities expose your schema and tie the API to it.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: DTOs decouple the API from the schema and avoid leaking fields.

questions.explanation: Entities can leak internal columns, trigger lazy-loading problems during serialisation, and let clients set fields they should not. The same applies to FastAPI: use response_model with a Pydantic schema, not the ORM object.

questions.prompt: Select all statements about centralised error handling that are true.

options.text: A @RestControllerAdvice class with @ExceptionHandler methods maps exceptions for every controller.
options.why: Right: advice applies globally by default.

options.text: Spring Framework 6 and Boot 3 can return a ProblemDetail, the standard problem-details format (RFC 9457, formerly 7807).
options.why: Right: it gives a consistent JSON error shape.

options.text: In FastAPI, raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Not found") returns that status with a JSON body {"detail": ...}.
options.why: Right: this is the built-in way to signal an HTTP error.

options.text: In FastAPI, @app.exception_handler(MyError) maps a custom exception to a response you build.
options.why: Right: the handler receives the request and the exception.

options.text: An @ExceptionHandler method declared in one controller also handles exceptions from every other controller.
options.why: It only applies to its own controller unless placed in advice.

questions.explanation: Throw domain exceptions from services and translate them in one place. That keeps controllers thin and error responses consistent.

questions.prompt: You must time every method in the service layer, including calls made by a scheduled job and a message listener that never go through an HTTP request. Which Spring mechanism fits?

options.text: A Servlet Filter registered for all URL patterns.
options.why: Filters only see HTTP requests, so jobs and listeners are missed.

options.text: A HandlerInterceptor with preHandle and afterCompletion.
options.why: Interceptors wrap MVC handler calls only, not service-to-service calls.

options.text: A @ControllerAdvice class with an @ExceptionHandler method.
options.why: It handles thrown exceptions in controllers, not timing.

options.text: An @Aspect with @Around advice on the service package.
options.why: Right: AOP wraps bean method calls whatever the caller is.

questions.explanation: Filters (and FastAPI middleware) wrap the whole HTTP request; interceptors see the chosen handler; AOP wraps method calls on Spring beans, though self-invocation inside a class bypasses the proxy. In FastAPI, per-route cross-cutting work is usually a dependency.
